subject: biology
title: Gene regulation
summary: How cells switch genes on and off, using the trp operon in E. coli as the model of repression and attenuation.
body:
Almost every cell in your body carries the same genes, yet a liver cell and a nerve cell make very different proteins. This is possible because cells control which genes are expressed, when, and how much. This lesson explains why gene regulation matters and uses the **trp operon** of the bacterium *Escherichia coli* (*E. coli*) to show, step by step, how a cell switches a set of genes off when it does not need them.

## Think of it like this

### Every cell has the same streaming library, but watches different shows

Everyone in your family might share one streaming account with thousands of shows, yet each person only watches a few. Every cell in your body has the same genes (the full library), but a liver cell and a nerve cell "play" different ones. That is **gene regulation**: controlling whether, when and how much a gene is expressed. **Regulatory genes** are like the parental controls and watch lists that decide what gets played, while **structural genes** are the shows themselves, the working proteins such as enzymes and haemoglobin.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* a person chooses a show on purpose, but cells have no decision-maker; regulation happens through molecules such as **repressor proteins** and **transcription factors** binding (or not binding) to DNA.

### The trp operon is like a canteen that stops baking when the pie warmer is full

The school canteen keeps baking pies (the **trp operon** is normally **on**) until the pie warmer is full. When there are plenty of pies, a pie is handed to the manager (**tryptophan** binds the **trp repressor**), and that is the signal that switches the manager into "stop" mode (the repressor changes shape and becomes active). The manager then stands in the kitchen doorway (binds the **operator**) so the baker (**RNA polymerase**) can't get to the ovens (the **structural genes**). As pies sell out, the manager no longer holds a pie, steps aside, and baking starts again. More product means less production: **negative feedback** in a **repressible operon**.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* the manager is always there, but the analogy can make it sound like the repressor appears only when needed; in fact *trpR* makes repressor all the time, and tryptophan never touches the DNA itself.

### Attenuation is like a zip that can close two different ways

Picture the **leader sequence** mRNA as a jacket with a zip that has four sections, where section 3 can zip onto either section 2 or section 4. The **ribosome** is a hand running along the jacket. If tryptophan is plentiful, the hand moves fast and covers section 2, so 3 zips onto 4 and forms the **terminator hairpin**, which pushes RNA polymerase off. If tryptophan is scarce, the hand **stalls** at section 1, section 2 is free to zip onto 3 (the **anti-terminator**), and transcription carries on into the genes.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* a zip is mechanical, but the "zipping" is complementary base pairing within one RNA strand, and it only works because in bacteria translation starts while transcription is still happening.

### In real life

The same switching idea is used in biotechnology: scientists put a gene next to a promoter they can turn on or off, so bacteria make a useful protein only when told to. Many antibiotics also work by interfering with bacterial transcription or translation, which are different enough from ours to be targeted.

## Key ideas

### Why cells regulate genes

**Gene regulation** is the control of whether, when and how much a gene is expressed. Cells regulate their genes because:

- **It saves energy and materials.** Transcription and translation use a lot of ATP, nucleotides and amino acids. Making a protein that is not needed wastes resources a cell could use to grow and divide.
- **It lets cells respond to their environment.** A bacterium can make enzymes to use a nutrient only when that nutrient is present, or make an amino acid only when it is missing from its surroundings.
- **It allows cells to specialise.** In multicellular organisms, different cell types express different sets of genes. This is how cells **differentiate** into muscle, skin, blood and so on, even though they share the same DNA.
- **It controls development.** Genes must be turned on and off in the right order and place for an embryo to develop its body plan.

### Structural and regulatory genes

Genes can be grouped by the role of their product.

- **Structural genes** code for proteins (or RNA) used in the structure or everyday functioning of the cell, such as enzymes, transport proteins, haemoglobin or keratin.
- **Regulatory genes** code for products that control the expression of other genes. Many regulatory genes code for proteins that bind to DNA and switch genes on or off. Examples include **repressor proteins**, which block transcription, and **activator proteins** or **transcription factors**, which help RNA polymerase start transcription.

In short: structural genes make the cell's working proteins; regulatory genes decide when those proteins are made.

### Operons in prokaryotes

In prokaryotes, genes for proteins that work together are often grouped into an **operon**: a cluster of structural genes controlled by a single promoter and operator, and transcribed together as one mRNA. The parts of an operon are:

- **Promoter** — where RNA polymerase binds.
- **Operator** — a DNA sequence next to (and overlapping) the promoter where a repressor can bind.
- **Structural genes** — the genes that code for the enzymes.

The regulatory gene that codes for the repressor is *not* part of the operon. It has its own promoter and is usually located elsewhere on the chromosome.

Operons make sense for bacteria because they can switch on or off a whole pathway of enzymes with a single control point.

### The trp operon: repression

**Tryptophan** (trp) is an amino acid that *E. coli* needs to make proteins. It can either absorb tryptophan from its surroundings or make it using a series of five enzymes. The genes for these enzymes (named *trpE*, *trpD*, *trpC*, *trpB* and *trpA*) form the **trp operon**.

The operon is controlled by a regulatory gene called ***trpR***, which codes for the **trp repressor** protein. The repressor is made all the time, but on its own it is **inactive**: its shape does not allow it to bind to the operator.

**When tryptophan is low (scarce):**

1. The trp repressor stays inactive and does not bind the operator.
2. RNA polymerase binds the promoter and moves freely through the operator.
3. The five structural genes are transcribed into one mRNA and translated into the five enzymes.
4. The cell makes its own tryptophan. The operon is **on**.

**When tryptophan is high (plentiful):**

1. Tryptophan molecules bind to the trp repressor. Tryptophan is acting as a **corepressor**, a small molecule that activates a repressor.
2. Binding changes the repressor's shape so it can now bind tightly to the operator.
3. The bound repressor physically blocks RNA polymerase from transcribing the structural genes.
4. No enzymes are made, so the cell stops wasting energy making tryptophan it already has. The operon is **off**.

Because the operon is normally on and is switched off by its end product, the trp operon is called a **repressible operon**. It is a good example of **negative feedback**: the more product there is, the less is made.

### The trp operon: attenuation

Repression does not shut the operon off completely, because the repressor binds and releases the operator. *E. coli* has a second, finer control called **attenuation**, which stops transcription early when tryptophan levels are high.

Between the operator and the first structural gene is a short **leader sequence** (*trpL*). Its mRNA has four regions (1, 2, 3 and 4) that can fold by complementary base pairing into hairpin loops. Region 1 also codes for a short **leader peptide** that contains two tryptophan codons side by side.

Attenuation works because in bacteria a ribosome starts translating the mRNA while RNA polymerase is still transcribing it.

**When tryptophan is high:**

1. Plenty of tRNA carrying tryptophan is available, so the ribosome moves quickly through the trp codons in region 1.
2. The ribosome covers region 2, so region 2 cannot pair with anything.
3. Region 3 pairs with region 4, forming a **terminator hairpin** (attenuator).
4. This hairpin causes RNA polymerase to detach before it reaches the structural genes. Transcription stops.

**When tryptophan is low:**

1. Little tRNA carrying tryptophan is available, so the ribosome **stalls** at the trp codons in region 1.
2. Region 2 is left uncovered and pairs with region 3, forming an **anti-terminator hairpin**.
3. Because region 3 is already paired, the 3–4 terminator cannot form.
4. RNA polymerase continues into the structural genes, and the enzymes are made.

Repression responds to free tryptophan binding the repressor; attenuation responds to how much tryptophan is loaded on tRNA. Together they give the cell very fine control.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: Predicting the effect of a mutation in *trpR*

A mutant *E. coli* has a mutation in *trpR* so its repressor cannot bind tryptophan. The bacteria are grown with plenty of tryptophan. Predict and explain whether the trp enzymes are made.

1. Normally, high tryptophan activates the repressor by binding to it.
2. In the mutant, tryptophan cannot bind, so the repressor stays inactive and cannot bind the operator.
3. RNA polymerase is not blocked, so the operon is transcribed (although attenuation would still reduce transcription to some extent).
4. Prediction: the enzymes are still made even though tryptophan is plentiful, which wastes energy.

### Example 2: Predicting the effect of an operator mutation

A different mutant has a change in the operator sequence so that even an active repressor cannot bind to it. What happens in low and high tryptophan?

1. Low tryptophan: the repressor is inactive anyway, so the operon is on, as normal.
2. High tryptophan: the repressor is active but cannot bind the changed operator. RNA polymerase is not blocked.
3. Repression no longer works in either condition. Only attenuation can reduce expression when tryptophan is high.

### Example 3: Interpreting data

Researchers measured the activity of the first trp enzyme in normal *E. coli* grown in two media.

| Medium | Enzyme activity |
|---|---|
| No tryptophan added | High |
| Tryptophan added | Very low |

Explain the results.

1. With no tryptophan added, the cell must make its own. The repressor is inactive, the ribosome stalls on the leader so the anti-terminator forms, and the operon is fully transcribed. Enzyme activity is high.
2. With tryptophan added, tryptophan activates the repressor, which binds the operator, and any transcripts that do start are mostly ended early by attenuation. Few enzymes are made, so activity is very low.

## Common mistakes

- Saying tryptophan binds to the operator. Tryptophan binds to the repressor; the activated repressor binds to the operator.
- Saying the repressor gene (*trpR*) is part of the operon. It is a separate regulatory gene with its own promoter.
- Thinking the repressor is only made when tryptophan is high. The repressor is made all the time; tryptophan only activates it.
- Mixing up which hairpin forms. High tryptophan → ribosome moves on → 3–4 terminator forms → transcription stops. Low tryptophan → ribosome stalls → 2–3 anti-terminator forms → transcription continues.
- Describing attenuation as happening in eukaryotes. It relies on transcription and translation happening at the same time, which happens in prokaryotes.

## Exam tips

- For repression, describe the chain of events in order: tryptophan level → repressor shape → binding to operator → RNA polymerase blocked or not → enzymes made or not.
- For attenuation, say what the ribosome does (moves quickly or stalls), which regions pair, and whether RNA polymerase continues.
- Mutation questions are common. Work out which part is broken (repressor, operator, promoter or leader) and trace the effect in both high and low tryptophan.
- Always link back to why: regulation conserves energy and resources.

## Tips to remember

- **"Enough already!"**: the trp operon is normally on. When the cell has plenty of tryptophan, tryptophan itself says "stop making me" by switching the repressor on. That is negative feedback in a repressible operon.
- **Key and lock-down chain** (a made-up memory trick): **T**ryptophan binds the **R**epressor, the **R**epressor binds the **O**perator, RNA polymerase is **B**locked. Think "T-R-O-B": tryptophan never touches the DNA itself.
- **Promoter = parking spot, operator = boom gate**: RNA polymerase parks at the promoter; an active repressor sitting on the operator is a closed boom gate that stops it driving into the genes.
- **The repressor is always made, just switched off**: *trpR* is a separate regulatory gene, outside the operon, making repressor all the time. Tryptophan only changes its shape so it can bind.
- **Attenuation, "Stall = go on, speed = stop"**: low tryptophan, the ribosome **stalls** on region 1, regions 2–3 pair (anti-terminator) and transcription **continues**. High tryptophan, the ribosome **speeds** over region 2, regions 3–4 pair (terminator) and transcription **stops**. Think "3–4, shut the door".
- **Quick self-check for mutation questions**: name the broken part (repressor, operator, promoter or leader), then trace what happens in BOTH high and low tryptophan.

## Key terms

- **Gene regulation** — control of whether, when and how much a gene is expressed.
- **Structural gene** — gene coding for a protein used in cell structure or function.
- **Regulatory gene** — gene coding for a product that controls the expression of other genes.
- **Operon** — cluster of prokaryotic structural genes under one promoter and operator, transcribed together.
- **Operator** — DNA sequence where a repressor binds to block transcription.
- **Repressor protein** — protein that binds to an operator and prevents transcription.
- **Corepressor** — small molecule (here, tryptophan) that binds and activates a repressor.
- **Repressible operon** — operon that is normally on and is switched off by a corepressor.
- **Attenuation** — early stopping of transcription caused by a terminator hairpin forming in the leader mRNA.
- **Leader sequence** — region between the operator and the first structural gene that controls attenuation.

## Summary

- Cells regulate genes to save energy and materials, respond to their environment, specialise and develop.
- Structural genes code for working proteins; regulatory genes code for products, such as repressors, that control other genes.
- The trp operon contains five structural genes for tryptophan synthesis under one promoter and operator.
- When tryptophan is high, it binds and activates the trp repressor, which binds the operator and blocks RNA polymerase.
- Attenuation adds fine control: high tryptophan lets a 3–4 terminator hairpin form so transcription stops early; low tryptophan causes ribosome stalling and a 2–3 anti-terminator so transcription continues.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is the best description of a regulatory gene?

options.A: A gene that codes for an enzyme in a metabolic pathway
options.B: A gene that codes for a product controlling the expression of other genes
options.C: A DNA sequence where a repressor protein binds
options.D: A section of a gene that is spliced out of pre-mRNA

questions.explanation: Regulatory genes code for products, such as repressor proteins, that switch other genes on or off. Option C describes the operator, which is a binding site, not a gene that codes for anything. Option A describes a structural gene.

questions.prompt: In the trp operon of E. coli, the trp repressor protein is coded for by

options.A: trpE, the first structural gene of the operon.

questions.explanation: The repressor is coded by trpR, a regulatory gene with its own promoter outside the operon. Option B is tempting because the repressor binds to the operator, but the operator is only a binding site and codes for no protein.

questions.prompt: What is the role of tryptophan in regulating the trp operon?

options.A: It acts as a corepressor, binding to the repressor and changing its shape so it can bind the operator.
options.B: It binds directly to the operator and blocks RNA polymerase.
options.C: It binds to the promoter and attracts RNA polymerase.
options.D: It inactivates the repressor so the operon is switched on.

questions.explanation: Tryptophan binds to the trp repressor, changing its shape so the repressor can attach to the operator and block transcription. Option B is the most common error: tryptophan never binds DNA directly. Option D describes an inducer in a different kind of operon, not tryptophan's role here.

questions.prompt: Which statement best explains why E. coli regulates the trp operon?

options.A: Tryptophan is toxic to E. coli, so its production must be blocked.
options.B: The trp enzymes can only be made when tryptophan is present.
options.C: Regulation prevents mutations in the trp genes.
options.D: Making the enzymes when tryptophan is already available would waste energy and materials.

questions.explanation: The cell avoids spending ATP, nucleotides and amino acids on enzymes it does not need when tryptophan is plentiful. Option B has the logic backwards: the enzymes are made when tryptophan is absent, because that is when the cell needs to make its own.

questions.prompt: During attenuation of the trp operon, why does the ribosome stall at the leader sequence when tryptophan levels are low?

options.A: The repressor binds to the ribosome and stops it.
options.B: There is little tRNA carrying tryptophan to pair with the trp codons in region 1.
options.C: The leader sequence contains a stop codon that is only read in low tryptophan.
options.D: RNA polymerase has stopped transcribing so there is no mRNA to read.

questions.explanation: Region 1 contains two tryptophan codons. When tryptophan is scarce, few tRNAs are loaded with it, so the ribosome waits at these codons. Option A wrongly links the repressor to attenuation; the repressor acts on DNA at the operator, not on ribosomes.

questions.prompt: A mutant E. coli produces a trp repressor that is always active, even without tryptophan. In a medium with no tryptophan, the bacteria would most likely

options.A: make high levels of trp enzymes because tryptophan is absent.
options.B: make high levels of trp enzymes because attenuation is switched off.
options.C: make very few trp enzymes and grow poorly because they cannot make their own tryptophan.
options.D: make normal levels of trp enzymes because the operator is unchanged.

questions.explanation: An always-active repressor stays bound to the operator, blocking RNA polymerase regardless of tryptophan level, so the cell cannot make the enzymes it needs and struggles to grow. Option A describes what normal bacteria do; it ignores the effect of the mutation.

questions.prompt: A mutation in the trp leader sequence prevents region 3 from pairing with region 4. What is the most likely effect when tryptophan is high and the repressor is not bound at that moment?

options.A: Transcription continues into the structural genes because the terminator hairpin cannot form.
options.B: Transcription stops early because the anti-terminator cannot form.
options.C: The ribosome stalls at region 1, stopping transcription.
options.D: The repressor can no longer bind tryptophan.

questions.explanation: The 3–4 hairpin is the terminator that ends transcription early in high tryptophan. Without it, RNA polymerase carries on into the structural genes. Option B is tempting but the anti-terminator is the 2–3 hairpin, and its absence would not stop transcription. The leader mutation has no effect on the repressor.

questions.prompt: Researchers find that a mutant E. coli makes trp enzymes at high levels whether or not tryptophan is present, and the trp repressor protein is normal. Which mutation best explains this?

options.A: A mutation in the promoter that prevents RNA polymerase binding
options.B: A mutation in trpR that makes the repressor always active
options.C: A mutation in trpE that changes the shape of the first enzyme
options.D: A mutation in the operator that prevents the active repressor from binding

questions.explanation: If the repressor is normal but cannot attach to the operator, RNA polymerase is never blocked, so the operon stays on even in high tryptophan. Option A would stop all expression, the opposite of what is seen. Option B is ruled out because the repressor is stated to be normal, and an always-active repressor would switch the operon off.
